14        Plaintiff Valeo Schalter und Sensoren GmbH (“Valeo”) moves for issuance of a letter of 
15   request for documents under the Hague Evidence Convention to non-party Mercedes-Benz Group 
16   AG (“Mercedes”) in Stuttgart, Germany.  Dkt. Nos. 151, 152.1  Defendant NVIDIA Corporation 
17   (“NVIDIA”) opposes the motion.  Dkt. No. 161.  The Court held oral argument on the motion on 
18   January 7, 2025.  Dkt. No. 180.                                       
19        Having considered the moving and responding papers and the parties’ arguments at the 
20   hearing, the Court denies Valeo’s motion.                             
21   I.   BACKGROUND                                                       
22        Valeo employed Mr. Mohamed Shawki Elamir as a systems engineer in Germany for 
23   several years until he left the company in December 2021.  See Dkt. No. 161-3 at ECF 3.  In 
24   January 2022, Mr. Elamir began work as a senior systems engineer for Mercedes, also in

27   principally to Valeo’s separately filed memorandum at Dkt. No. 152, and not the motion at Dkt. 
1   Germany.  See id. at ECF 2.  At some point (perhaps in 2024), Mr. Elamir left Mercedes and 
2   joined NVIDIA.  See Dkt. No. 152 at 1; Dkt. No. 164 at 2 (referring to edits in NVIDIA code 
3   made by Mr. Elamir in July 2024).                                     
4        Meanwhile, in early 2021, Mercedes awarded NVIDIA a contract to provide certain 
5   software for advanced parking and driving assistance to Mercedes.  See Dkt. No. 152 at 2; Dkt. 
6   No. 1 ¶¶ 9-10, 50, 53.  At the same time, Mercedes awarded Valeo a contract to provide ultrasonic 
7   sensors for advanced parking and driving assistance to Mercedes.  Dkt. No. 1 ¶¶ 9-11, 49-51. 
8        Valeo filed a motion for issuance of a letter of request on November 18, 2024.  Dkt. No. 
9   152.  The motion asks the Court to issue a letter of request under Article 3 of the Hague Evidence 
10   Convention asking the German Central Authority to “cause Mercedes-Benz Group AG to 
11   produce” several categories of documents.  Dkt. No. 152-1 at 6.  The proposed letter of request 
12   recites that “[t]he evidence sought has a direct and necessary link with the civil lawsuit over which 
13   [the Court] is currently presiding, and it is expected to be offered as evidence at trial in this 
14   matter.”  Id. at 1.  In addition, the proposed letter states that the request “is of an urgent nature as 
15   the discovery in this matter will close on December 18th, 2024,” and asks that “the requested 
16   documents be produced by at least December 18th, 2024, or as early thereafter as possible.”  Id. at 
17   2.                                                                    
18        In support of its motion, Valeo makes the following assertions “on information and belief”: 
19        •  “[A]fter failing to independently develop the technology needed for advanced driver 
20          assistance systems, NVIDIA brazenly recruited and induced two former Valeo 
21          employees to steal Valeo’s trade secrets.”  Dkt. No. 152 at 1. 
22        •  “[Mr. Elamir], started working for NVIDIA just days after the first employee [Mr. 
23          Moniruzzaman] was terminated, and is picking up where the other left off.”  Id. 
24        •  “[T]hese two employees were hired by NVIDIA notwithstanding reservations about 
25          their skills . . . because they would bring over Valeo’s trade secrets and know-how 
26          when recruited by NVIDIA.”  Id. at 1-2.                        
27        •  “[D]uring the Mercedes OEM project (“OEM project”), NVIDIA encountered multiple 
1        •  “Mercedes and Elamir, who was a Mercedes employee at the time, would have 
2          documented, discussed, and evaluated the capabilities and faults of NVIDIA’s parking 
3          and driving assistance technology to determine how it would affect the timelines for, 
4          and the success and profitability of, the OEM project.”  Id.   
5        In its reply, Valeo additionally asserts that it discovered in July 2024 that “Mr. Elamir 
6   implemented Valeo trade secrets in NVIDIA’s source code in the July 3, 2024 version made 
7   available for review.”  Dkt. No. 164 at 2.  According to Valeo, in late August 2024, NVIDIA 
8   produced notes from its employment interviews with Mr. Elamir.  Id.  And in late October 2024, 
9   NVIDIA identified additional documents regarding its recruitment and hiring of Mr. Elamir, 
10   although Valeo suggests the production was deficient.  Id. at 2-3.    
11   II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                   
12        The Hague Convention on the Taking of Evidence Abroad in Civil or Commercial Matters, 
13   March 8, 1970, 23 U.S.T. 2555, T.I.A.S. No. 7444 (“Hague Evidence Convention” or 
14   “Convention”), “prescribes certain procedures by which a judicial authority in one contracting 
15   state may request evidence located in another contracting state.”  Societe Nationale Industrielle 
16   Aerospatiale v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for S. Dist. of Iowa, 482 U.S. 522, 524 (1987).  A federal district 
17   court may transmit a “letter of request” for evidence directly to the Central Authority designated 
18   by another party to the Convention for execution.  See Hague Evidence Convention, Art. 2; 28 
19   U.S.C. § 1781(b)(2).  The United States and Germany are both signatories to the Convention.  See 
20   https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-table/?cid=82.   
21        Where the requirements of the Convention are met, courts in the Ninth Circuit generally 
22   grant motions requesting issuance of a letter of request, unless the opposing party identifies a good 
23   reason to deny the application.  See Successor Agency to Former Emeryville Redevelopment 
24   Agency v. Swagelok Co., No. 17-cv-00308-WHO, 2020 WL 7042860, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 1, 
25   2020) (citing S.E.C. v. Leslie, 07-cv-03444 JF (PVT), 2009 WL 688836, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 16, 
26   2009)); see also WebPros Int’l, LLC v. Asli, No. 22-cv-01963-IM, 2024 WL 3064985, at *2 (D. 
27   Or. June 20, 2024) (summarizing cases).  Like all discovery, such motions must comply with the 
1   nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party’s claim or defense.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b).  
2   Likewise, a motion for issuance of a letter of request is subject to the case management schedule 
3   set by the district court.                                            
4   III.  DISCUSSION                                                      
5        NVIDIA objects to issuance of Valeo’s proposed letter of request on the ground that Valeo 
6   unduly delayed bringing its motion, such that the documents it seeks could not be obtained until 
7   after the close of fact discovery.  In addition, the Court raised sua sponte whether the proposed 
8   letter of request complies with the requirements of the Hague Evidence Convention, in view of 
9   Germany’s declarations.  The Court address both issues.               
10        A.   Whether Valeo’s Motion Is Untimely                          
11        Civil Local Rule 37-3 provides that “[d]iscovery requests that call for responses . . . after 
12   the applicable discovery cut-off are not enforceable, except by order of the Court for good cause 
13   shown.”  Civil L.R. 37-3.  NVIDIA observes that because Valeo did not file its motion until 
14   November 18, 2024, one month before the December 18, 2024 close of fact discovery, the motion 
15   could not be heard, and the letter of request could not issue, until after the fact discovery cut-off.  
16   Dkt. No. 161 at 3-4; see also Civil L.R. 7-2(a) (requiring 35 days’ notice for hearings on motions). 
17        According to NVIDIA, Valeo has known since at least May 30, 2024 that its former 
18   employee, Mr. Elamir, worked on the same functionality that Mr. Moniruzzaman had previously 
19   worked on, see Dkt. No. 161 at 1; Dkt. No. 162-2 (amended response to Interrogatory No. 2), and 
20   Valeo has known “for years” that after Mr. Elamir left Valeo’s employ, he worked for Mercedes, 
21   see Dkt. No. 161 at 2; Dkt. No. 161-3.                                
22        Valeo does not dispute that since at least July 2024 it had knowledge of Mr. Elamir’s 
23   employment at Mercedes and his subsequent role at NVIDIA, including the specific work Mr. 
24   Elamir performed on NVIDIA’s source code.  See Dkt. No. 164 at 2.  Valeo’s arguments that it 
25   required more information regarding Mr. Elamir’s “recruitment and hiring” by NVIDIA before it 
26   could reasonably seek documents from Mercedes, see id. at 2, 4, are not persuasive for at least two 
27   reasons.  First, several of the document requests in Valeo’s proposed letter of request have nothing 
1   trade secrets in aid of NVIDIA’s performance of its contract with Mercedes.  See Dkt. No. 152 at 
2   3-5.  Yet, Valeo has known since early 2021 of NVIDIA’s contract to supply advanced parking 
3   and driving assistance software to Mercedes and that Mercedes would have information regarding 
4   NVIDIA’s performance of that contract.  See id. at 2; Dkt. No. 1 ¶¶ 9-10, 50, 53.  Second, to the 
5   extent Valeo seeks documents from Mercedes regarding Mr. Elamir’s observations and 
6   communications while employed there, Valeo has known for a long time that Mr. Elamir worked 
7   as a systems engineer on parking assistance technology for Mercedes, and Valeo concedes that it 
8   has known since July 2024 the nature of Mr. Elamir’s subsequent work for NVIDIA.  See Dkt. No. 
9   164 at 2.  In these circumstances, Valeo has not shown good cause for waiting until November 18, 
10   2024 to seek issuance of a letter of request directed to Mercedes, knowing that if the motion was 
11   granted, such letter would not be issued until after the December 18, 2024 close of fact discovery.2 
12        When pressed on the timing of its motion at the hearing, Valeo explained that its letter of 
13   request does not seek discovery, but rather impeachment evidence or evidence to refresh 
14   recollection at trial.  Dkt. No. 180.  However, while Valeo (like all litigants) may expect to use 
15   some of the documents it requests from Mercedes at trial, the letter of request does not identify 
16   any specific evidence in Mercedes’s possession, but instead describes categories of documents that 
17   may exist.  See Dkt. No. 152 at 3-4.  This is classic pretrial discovery.  Moreover, the proposed 
18   letter clearly contemplates obtaining any responsive documents as part of discovery.  See Dkt. No. 
19   152-1 at 2 (“This Letter of Request is of an urgent nature as the discovery in this matter will close 
20   on December 18th, 2024.”).                                            
21        The Court concludes that Valeo’s motion for issuance of a letter of request for documents 
22   in Mercedes’s possession was not timely filed, and no good cause excuses Valeo’s delay. 
23        B.   Whether Valeo’s Proposed Letter Complies with the Convention 
24        Even if the Court permitted Valeo to proceed with its motion at this late date, the proposed 
25   letter of request does not comply with the requirements of the Hague Evidence Convention as it 
26

1   has been implemented in Germany.                                      
2        Article 23 of the Hague Evidence Convention states:  “A Contracting State may at the time 
3   of signature, ratification or accession, declare that it will not execute Letters of Request issued for 
4   the purpose of obtaining pre-trial discovery of documents as known in Common Law countries.”  
5   23 U.S.T. 2555, T.I.A.S. No. 7444.  On April 27, 1979, Germany made the following declaration 
6   pursuant to Article 23 of the Convention:  “The Federal Republic of Germany declares in 
7   pursuance of Article 23 of the Convention that it will not, in its territory, execute Letters of 
8   Request issued for the purpose of obtaining pre-trial discovery of documents as known in common 
9   law countries.”  See https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-
10   table/notifications/?csid=502&disp=resdn.  On July 28, 2022, Germany amended its Article 23 
11   declaration, as follows:                                              
12             A Letter of Request issued for the purpose of obtaining pre-trial 
              discovery of documents pursuant to Article 23 of the Convention 
13                                                                         
              shall only be executed if                                   
14               1.  the documents requested are described separately in detail, 
15               2.  the documents requested are of immediate and clearly  
                   recognisable relevance for the respective proceedings and 
16                  their outcome,                                         
17               3.  the documents requested are in the possession of a party to 
                   the proceedings,                                       
18                                                                         
                4.  the Letter of Request does not violate fundamental principles 
19                  of German law[,] and                                   
                5.  to the extent the documents requested contain personal data, 
20                                                                         
                   the requirements for the transfer of personal data to a third 
21                  country pursuant to Chapter V of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 
                   of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 
22                  2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the 
                   processing of personal data and on the free movement of 
23                  such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data 
                   Protection Regulation) (OJ L 119, 4 May 2016, p.1; L 314, 
24                                                                         
                   22 November 2016, p. 2; L 127, 23 May 2018, p. 2; L 74, 4 
25                  March 2021, p. 35) are met.                            
26   See id.                                                               
27        Valeo does not address Germany’s current Article 23 declaration in its motion, even 
1   See generally Dkt. No. 152.  However, a review of the document requests directed to Mercedes 
2   reveals that the proposed letter of request does not meet the criteria in Germany’s Article 23 
3   declaration.  The documents sought are not “described separately in detail”; rather, categories of 
4   documents that may exist are described collectively.  The documents sought are not “in the 
5   possession of a party to the proceedings”; Mercedes is a non-party.  In addition, Valeo has not 
6   demonstrated that “the documents requested are of immediate and clearly [recognizable] relevance 
7   for” the trial in this action.  To the contrary, most of Valeo’s assertions in support of the proposed 
8   letter are made “on information and belief,” suggesting that it does not have any firm basis to 
9   conclude any of the documents it seeks actually exist.  And even if, for example, Mercedes had a 
10   document showing it considered terminating NVIDIA’s contract due to problems or delays, it is 
11   not immediately clear that such information is relevant to this action.  Rather, Valeo speculates 
12   that, if NVIDIA experienced problems or delays, it might have had a motive to hire former Valeo 
13   employees to fix its problems and help it catch up by misappropriating Valeo’s trade secrets.  
14        At the hearing, Valeo argued that it is not seeking pretrial discovery of Mercedes, and so 
15   the limitations in Germany’s Article 23 declaration do not apply.  For the reasons explained above, 
16   the Court is not persuaded that Valeo seeks only trial evidence and not pretrial discovery.  The 
17   proposed letter of request clearly seeks pretrial discovery of non-party Mercedes.  But even if the 
18   Court were to accept Valeo’s representation during the hearing that whatever documents it obtains 
19   from Mercedes will be used only for impeachment or refreshing recollection of testimony Mr. 
20   Elamir may give at trial, Valeo does not identify any testimony by Mr. Elamir that Valeo 
21   anticipates might be subject to impeachment or that might require refreshing his recollection.  
22   Valeo acknowledged that it had an opportunity to depose Mr. Elamir during discovery in this 
23   action, but that it did not ask him about the matters described in Valeo’s proposed document 
24   requests to Mercedes.  Dkt. No. 180.                                  
25        The Court concludes that Valeo’s motion for issuance of a letter of request for documents 
26   in Mercedes’s possession does not comply with the requirements of the Hague Evidence 
27   Convention, in view of Germany’s Article 23 declaration.              
    1  |} IV.    CONCLUSION 
    2          For the reasons explained in this order, the Court denies Valeo’s motion for issuance of a 
    3    letter of request. 
    4          IT IS SO ORDERED.

1   See generally Dkt. No. 152.  However, a review of the document requests directed to Mercedes 
2   reveals that the proposed letter of request does not meet the criteria in Germany’s Article 23 
3   declaration.  The documents sought are not “described separately in detail”; rather, categories of 
4   documents that may exist are described collectively.  The documents sought are not “in the 
5   possession of a party to the proceedings”; Mercedes is a non-party.  In addition, Valeo has not 
6   demonstrated that “the documents requested are of immediate and clearly [recognizable] relevance 
7   for” the trial in this action.  To the contrary, most of Valeo’s assertions in support of the proposed 
8   letter are made “on information and belief,” suggesting that it does not have any firm basis to 
9   conclude any of the documents it seeks actually exist.  And even if, for example, Mercedes had a 
10   document showing it considered terminating NVIDIA’s contract due to problems or delays, it is 
11   not immediately clear that such information is relevant to this action.  Rather, Valeo speculates 
12   that, if NVIDIA experienced problems or delays, it might have had a motive to hire former Valeo 
13   employees to fix its problems and help it catch up by misappropriating Valeo’s trade secrets.  
14        At the hearing, Valeo argued that it is not seeking pretrial discovery of Mercedes, and so 
15   the limitations in Germany’s Article 23 declaration do not apply.  For the reasons explained above, 
16   the Court is not persuaded that Valeo seeks only trial evidence and not pretrial discovery.  The 
17   proposed letter of request clearly seeks pretrial discovery of non-party Mercedes.  But even if the 
18   Court were to accept Valeo’s representation during the hearing that whatever documents it obtains 
19   from Mercedes will be used only for impeachment or refreshing recollection of testimony Mr. 
20   Elamir may give at trial, Valeo does not identify any testimony by Mr. Elamir that Valeo 
21   anticipates might be subject to impeachment or that might require refreshing his recollection.  
22   Valeo acknowledged that it had an opportunity to depose Mr. Elamir during discovery in this 
23   action, but that it did not ask him about the matters described in Valeo’s proposed document 
24   requests to Mercedes.  Dkt. No. 180.                                  
25        The Court concludes that Valeo’s motion for issuance of a letter of request for documents 
26   in Mercedes’s possession does not comply with the requirements of the Hague Evidence 
27   Convention, in view of Germany’s Article 23 declaration.
